reason: The provided sources give rich, cross-verified detail on Mariner 9's launch drama, planetary dust storm twist, reprogrammability triumph over Soviet probes, and major Martian discoveries.
story: In May 1971, NASA launched Mariner 9 to attempt history's first orbit of another planet, just weeks after its twin Mariner 8 plunged into the Atlantic Ocean. Reaching Mars in November 1971, Mariner 9 arrived first ahead of Soviet probes, only to find the entire Red Planet blinded by a colossal, planet-wide dust storm. While Soviet craft blindly took useless photographs of dust due to fixed pre-programming, NASA controllers reprogrammed Mariner 9 from Earth to wait out the tempest. When the dust finally cleared in early 1972, Mariner 9 revealed a dynamic world: gargantuan extinct volcanoes like Olympus Mons, ancient dried riverbeds suggesting past liquid water, and a 2,500-mile canyon system named Valles Marineris in its honor. By transmitting 7,329 photos and mapping 85% of the surface, Mariner 9 transformed our understanding of Mars and paved the way for future landers.
angle: When Mariner 9 arrived as the first probe to orbit another planet, Mars was engulfed in a planet-wide dust storm—forcing NASA to reprogram the craft from Earth while Soviet probes blindly took pictures of pure dust.

claims.claim: Mariner 9 launched on May 30, 1971, from Cape Canaveral, Florida, aboard an Atlas-Centaur rocket.
Mariner 9's twin spacecraft, Mariner 8, failed shortly after launch on May 9, 1971, and crashed into the Atlantic Ocean.
Mariner 8 crashed in the ocean roughly 350 miles (563 km) north to northwest of Puerto Rico.
Mariner 9 entered orbit around Mars on November 14, 1971, becoming the first spacecraft to orbit another planet.
Upon arrival, Mariner 9 found Mars obscured by a giant planet-wide dust storm.
NASA controllers reprogrammed Mariner 9's computer from Earth to delay surface imaging until the dust settled in early 1972.
The Soviet Union's Mars 2 and Mars 3 probes arrived during the same storm but could not adapt because their imaging systems were pre-programmed, returning photos of only dust.
Mariner 9 successfully mapped 85 percent of Mars's surface during its mission.
Mariner 9 returned 7,329 images of Mars back to Earth.
Mariner 9 discovered massive extinct volcanoes on Mars, including Olympus Mons.
Mariner 9 discovered a 2,500-mile (4,000 km) long canyon system that was later named Valles Marineris in honor of the spacecraft.
Mariner 9 captured close-up images of Mars's two small moons, Phobos and Deimos.
Mariner 9 photographed dried riverbeds and channels on Mars, suggesting liquid water had once flowed across the surface.
NASA turned off Mariner 9 on October 27, 1972, after the spacecraft ran out of attitude control gas.
Mariner 9 weighed more than the Mariner 6 and Mariner 7 spacecraft combined.
The imagery and data collected by Mariner 9 directly helped select landing sites and plan the Viking lander missions.

disputed: Orbital entry date discrepancy: EBSCOhost (S6) claims Mariner 9 achieved orbit on September 22, 1971, whereas Wikipedia (S1), NASA (S2), Space.com (S4), and Linda Hall Library (S7) state it entered orbit on November 14, 1971. The script should use November 14, 1971.

Mariner 9 crash/impact status: NASA and sources note predictions that Mariner 9 would crash into Mars around 2020 or 2022, but S7 notes there is no proof it actually did so yet. The script should describe it as expected to crash due to orbital decay rather than stating a confirmed crash date.

Conclusive proof of past water: S4 and S6 state Mariner 9 provided evidence/indications that water once flowed on Mars, while S2 notes spacecraft data could not provide conclusive proof. The script should describe the findings as strong evidence or indications of ancient flowing water.
